blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a key empirical study from ICSE '15 by Tufano et al. that examines when and why 'code smells' (symptoms of poor design or implementation choices) are introduced in software projects. The study analyzed over 500,000 commits across 200 open-source projects from Apache, Eclipse, and Android ecosystems, focusing on five types of smells including Blob Classes, Class Data Should be Private, and Spaghetti Code. The surprising finding is that most smells are introduced when a code entity is first added to the versioning system, rather than gradually over time as 'software ageing' theory might suggest. The paper also reveals that smells are predominantly introduced during enhancement operations (60-66%) and near release deadlines, with a significant portion (394 cases) even introduced during refactoring. Experienced file owners are more likely to introduce smells, likely due to performing more complex tasks. The study suggests potential for developing recommenders to warn developers about dangerous trends leading to smells.
paper_title: When and Why Your Code Starts to Smell Bad
paper_abstract: —Technical debt is a metaphor introduced by Cunningham to indicate “not quite right code which we postpone making it right”. One noticeable symptom of technical debt is represented by code smells, defined as symptoms of poor design and implementation choices. Previous studies showed the negative impact of code smells on the comprehensibility and maintainability of code. While the repercussions of smells on code quality have been empirically assessed, there is still only anecdotal evidence on when and why bad smells are introduced, what is their survivability, and how they are removed by developers. To empirically corroborate such anecdotal evidence, we conducted a large empirical study over the change history of 200 open source projects. This study required the development of a strategy to identify smell-introducing commits, the mining of over half a million of commits, and the manual analysis and classification of over 10K of them. Our findings mostly contradict common wisdom, showing that most of the smell instances are introduced when an artifact is created and not as a result of its evolution. At the same time, 80% of smells survive in the system. Also, among the 20% of removed instances, only 9% is removed as a direct consequence of refactoring operations. Index Terms—Code Smells, Empirical Study, Mining Software Repositories F
